subject: biology

items.q: Antarctic ice cores show that, over the last 800 000 years, periods of high global temperature coincided with high atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations and periods of low temperature with low concentrations. Which statement about this evidence is correct?
items.correct: It shows a positive correlation, but the causal link between carbon dioxide and temperature is established by other evidence.
items.misconception: It shows a positive correlation, which by itself proves that carbon dioxide raises global temperatures.
items.why: In everyday reasoning a consistent association is taken as proof, and school graphs of temperature against carbon dioxide are often presented as if the correlation were the whole argument. Data from Antarctic ice cores show a positive correlation between global temperatures and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations over hundreds of thousands of years. This correlation does not prove that carbon dioxide increases global temperatures; other evidence, including the physics of infrared absorption by carbon dioxide, confirms the causal link.
items.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
items.random_wrong: It shows a negative correlation in cold periods, when both variables fell, and a positive one in warm periods.

items.q: Which is an anthropogenic cause of the rise in the atmospheric concentration of methane since pre-industrial times?
items.correct: Enteric fermentation in the growing numbers of ruminant farm livestock
items.misconception: Exhalation of waste gases by the greatly increased human population
items.why: Students know from earlier courses that respiration releases carbon dioxide and that the human population has grown, and they connect the two without considering where the carbon in exhaled breath came from. The carbon in exhaled carbon dioxide was removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis only months or years earlier, so respiration returns carbon that was already cycling. The anthropogenic increase comes from adding carbon that had been locked away for millions of years in fossil fuels, from releasing stored carbon by deforestation and from cement production.
items.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
items.random_wrong: Complete combustion of coal and petroleum in vehicles and power stations

items.q: In a data set of 40 countries, the higher the percentage of electricity generated by burning coal, the higher the carbon dioxide emissions per person. In the same countries, the greater the percentage of land covered by forest, the lower the net carbon dioxide emissions. Based on these data alone, how should the two relationships be described?
items.correct: The first is a positive correlation and the second is a negative correlation
items.misconception: The first is a positive correlation and the second is a positive correlation too
items.why: Students read 'negative' and 'positive' as describing the direction of a trend over time, rather than the relationship between the two variables plotted against each other. The sign of a correlation describes how the two variables relate to each other, not whether either is rising or falling over time. If both variables fall together, that is a positive correlation; a negative correlation is one in which higher values of one variable go with lower values of the other.
items.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
items.random_wrong: The first is a strong correlation and the second is a much weaker correlation

items.q: Which process is part of a positive feedback cycle that increases global warming?
items.correct: Thawing permafrost releases methane gas into the atmosphere
items.misconception: More evaporation forms clouds that reflect sunlight and cool the surface
items.why: Students meet feedback first in homeostasis, where every example is stabilizing, and the everyday meaning of 'positive' suggests something helpful or corrective rather than something that amplifies. Negative feedback opposes a change and stabilizes a system. Positive feedback increases the change: in global warming, warming causes processes such as the release of methane from permafrost, which cause more warming.
items.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
items.random_wrong: Melting snow and ice absorb heat from their surroundings and cool the oceans

items.q: As the oceans warm, the amount of carbon dioxide that stays dissolved in the deep ocean changes. Why does this act as a positive feedback in global warming?
items.correct: Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so the warming ocean releases carbon dioxide, which enhances the greenhouse effect and warms the ocean further.
items.misconception: Gases are more soluble in warmer water, so the ocean takes up carbon dioxide and this stored gas traps heat in the water, warming it further.
items.why: Students generalize from solids such as sugar and salt, which dissolve faster and in greater amounts in hot water, without knowing that the solubility of gases falls as temperature rises. For gases the trend is the reverse of that for most solids: warm water holds less dissolved gas. As the deep ocean warms it releases carbon dioxide, which increases the greenhouse effect and causes further warming, a positive feedback cycle.
items.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
items.random_wrong: The carbon dioxide released returns the atmospheric concentration to its earlier value, which brings the temperature back to normal.

items.q: Fresh snow reflects about 85% of the solar radiation reaching it, whereas open ocean water reflects about 7%. Since 1980 the area of the Arctic Ocean covered by sea ice in September has fallen by more than 40%. What is the most likely consequence for the Arctic climate?
items.correct: The exposed dark water absorbs far more of the solar radiation, warming the region and melting still more ice.
items.misconception: Melting ice takes in heat from the water, so the Arctic Ocean is cooled and further loss of ice is slowed down.
items.why: Everyday experience of ice cooling a drink, and the physics idea that melting absorbs latent heat, both suggest that melting ice must be cooling its surroundings. The important effect is on albedo. Snow and ice reflect most incoming solar radiation, whereas open water and bare ground absorb most of it, so loss of snow and ice increases the absorption of solar radiation, warms the surface and melts more snow and ice.
items.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
items.random_wrong: The extra open water evaporates, and the cloud that forms reflects radiation and restores the ice cover.

items.q: Which sequence of events explains how boreal forests in a warming climate change from net carbon accumulation to net carbon loss?
items.correct: Warming and less winter snow cause drought, reduced primary production, forest browning and more fires that burn legacy carbon.
items.misconception: Warmer conditions and more carbon dioxide speed up photosynthesis, producing more litter, so decomposition releases more carbon than the trees fix.
items.why: Students learn that temperature and carbon dioxide concentration are limiting factors for photosynthesis, and expect raising both to increase growth, without considering water supply. In the taiga, warmer temperatures and decreased winter snowfall lead to drought. Water stress reduces primary production, causes forest browning and increases the frequency and intensity of forest fires, so the forest can pass a tipping point from net carbon accumulation to net loss.
items.specStatementText: Boreal forest: from carbon sink to carbon source
items.random_wrong: More frequent fires burn the trees, but regrowth reabsorbs that carbon, so the net loss comes only from timber removed by logging.

items.q: Researchers measured the carbon in the soil organic layer of a boreal forest after fires. In stands older than 70 years, the carbon that remained was older than the trees and had survived earlier fires. In stands younger than 60 years on drier sites, the fire had burnt through this old carbon. What do these results show?
items.correct: Fires in young stands on dry sites combust legacy carbon that older stands protect from burning.
items.misconception: Fires release only carbon fixed since the previous fire, so regrowth of the trees will restore the carbon balance.
items.why: Fire is taught as part of a natural cycle in fire-adapted forests, and students picture the carbon lost as the visible trees, not the deep soil organic layer. More frequent and more intense fires burn into soil organic layers that escaped previous fires, combusting legacy carbon that had accumulated over centuries. That carbon is not recovered before the next fire, so the forest becomes a net source of carbon.
items.specStatementText: Boreal forest: from carbon sink to carbon source
items.random_wrong: The forest has crossed a tipping point, so its carbon stock will recover gradually once the fires are out.

items.q: Emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) breed on landfast ice during the Antarctic winter, and the chicks fledge in December and January. Why does the early breakout of landfast ice threaten breeding?
items.correct: If the ice breaks out before the chicks have grown waterproof adult plumage, they fall into the sea and drown or die of cold.
items.misconception: The open water exposes the penguins to warmer air, which they cannot tolerate because they are adapted to cold.
items.why: Students think of climate change as animals 'getting too hot', because heat stress is the most obvious effect of warming on organisms. The polar warming involved is a few degrees; the threat is habitat change. Emperor penguins need landfast ice that lasts until their chicks fledge, and walruses need sea ice over the shallow shelf to rest between feeding dives. Losing the ice is losing the habitat.
items.specStatementText: Polar ice as habitat: emperor penguins and walruses
items.random_wrong: The melting ice raises the sea level and floods the colony on the shore where the eggs are being incubated.

items.q: Walruses (Odobenus rosmarus) feed on molluscs on the floor of the shallow Arctic continental shelf and rest on sea ice between dives. Summer sea ice now retreats into deep water beyond the shelf. What is the consequence for the walruses?
items.correct: They must haul out on land in large crowded groups and travel much further to reach their feeding grounds.
items.misconception: They move to the Antarctic, where the landfast ice still provides a resting platform close to the shelf.
items.why: Cartoons and advertisements routinely show penguins with polar bears or walruses, and 'polar' is treated as a single place. The two polar habitats have different faunas. The emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) breeds on Antarctic landfast ice; the walrus (Odobenus rosmarus) depends on Arctic sea ice. Neither occurs at the other pole.
items.specStatementText: Polar ice as habitat: emperor penguins and walruses
items.random_wrong: They overheat in the warmer water, because their thick blubber prevents them from losing heat quickly enough to survive.

items.q: Off the coast of Peru, cold nutrient-rich water normally rises to the surface. In some years the surface water is unusually warm, and the catch of anchovies falls sharply. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Warm surface water is less dense and does not mix with the water below, so fewer nutrients reach the surface and primary production falls.
items.misconception: Warm surface water raises the rate of enzyme activity in phytoplankton, which grow so fast that they use up all the oxygen the anchovies need.
items.why: Students apply the temperature–enzyme relationship learned for individual organisms to a whole ocean, without considering that nutrients, not temperature, limit phytoplankton growth in most surface waters. Phytoplankton in surface waters are usually limited by nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate. Warmer surface water is less dense and mixes less with the water below, so upwelling of nutrients is reduced, ocean primary production falls and less energy flows through marine food chains.
items.specStatementText: Warm surface water blocks nutrient upwelling
items.random_wrong: Phytoplankton obtain their nutrients from sunlight, so the fall in the catch must be caused by the greater cloud cover in the warmer years.

items.q: The bird species of a mountain in New Guinea were surveyed in 1965 and again in 2012. For most species both the upper and the lower limits of the altitudinal range had moved upslope, by about 100 m on average, over a period in which the region warmed. What is the best interpretation?
items.correct: The ranges of the species shifted upslope, tracking the rise in temperature.
items.misconception: The species have expanded their ranges, since they now occupy about 100 m more of the mountain.
items.why: The evidence students see first is the arrival of a species in a new place, and the retreat of the other edge of the range is less visible and less often reported. In the New Guinea bird surveys the upper and the lower limits of most species' ranges both moved upslope, and North American tree species show contraction at the southern edge alongside northward spread. A shift moves the range; it need not enlarge it.
items.specStatementText: Species move poleward and upslope
items.random_wrong: Because both limits moved equally, the species have lost none of their habitat area.

items.q: In a survey of forests in the eastern United States, seedlings of several northern tree species were found on average further north than mature trees of the same species, while at the southern edge of the range there were mature trees but few seedlings. What does this indicate?
items.correct: The ranges are shifting northward, with seedlings establishing beyond the northern edge and the range contracting at the southern edge.
items.misconception: The mature trees are themselves migrating northward as individuals, leaving the southern part of their range behind them.
items.why: Range shifts are taught alongside animal migration and students picture organisms relocating, which for rooted plants is impossible. For trees and most other organisms, a range shift is a population change over many generations: establishment of seedlings beyond one edge of the range and failure of reproduction or survival at the other edge.
items.specStatementText: Species move poleward and upslope
items.random_wrong: The species are expanding their ranges, since seedlings are appearing in the north while mature trees remain in the south.

items.q: Which statement correctly matches a threat to coral reefs with its cause?
items.correct: Suppression of calcification in corals is caused by the increased carbon dioxide concentration of seawater.
items.misconception: Coral bleaching is caused by ocean acidification, which dissolves the pigments out of the coral tissue.
items.why: Both threats are caused by carbon dioxide emissions and are taught together, and 'bleach' suggests a chemical, acid-like action rather than a response to heat. The two threats have different causes. Increased carbon dioxide concentration causes ocean acidification, which suppresses calcification. Increased water temperature causes bleaching: the stressed coral expels the algae that give it colour and most of its food.
items.specStatementText: Coral reefs: acidification and bleaching
items.random_wrong: Ocean acidification lowers the pH of seawater below 7, so the calcium carbonate skeletons of corals dissolve away.

items.q: During a marine heatwave, the corals on a reef turned white. When the water cooled four weeks later, most of the corals regained their colour. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Heat stress made the corals expel their zooxanthellae, and they took the algae up again once the stress had ended.
items.misconception: The corals died when they turned white, and the colour came from new corals that settled on the skeletons within four weeks.
items.why: Photographs of bleached and dead reefs look alike, and dead coral skeletons are white, so students equate the two. Bleaching is the expulsion of zooxanthellae by a living coral. The coral can survive for weeks and regain its algae if conditions improve; only prolonged or repeated bleaching leads to death and then to the collapse of the reef ecosystem.
items.specStatementText: Coral reefs: acidification and bleaching
items.random_wrong: The warm water became acidic and bleached the pigments, which re-formed once the pH returned to normal.

items.q: A drained peatland that had been releasing carbon dioxide is re-wetted so that the soil becomes waterlogged again. Why does this restoration act as an approach to carbon sequestration?
items.correct: Without oxygen, saprotrophs cannot decompose plant remains, which build up as peat
items.misconception: Waterlogging speeds up rotting, so plant remains turn into peat faster and store carbon
items.why: Everyday experience is that damp things rot, so students expect waterlogging to accelerate decomposition rather than prevent it. Saprotrophs need oxygen for aerobic respiration. Waterlogged soil is anaerobic, so decomposition is inhibited and plant material accumulates as peat, storing carbon; this occurs in temperate and boreal zones and very rapidly in some tropical ecosystems.
items.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
items.random_wrong: The cold of the water stops decomposition, so the carbon in plant remains stays stored

items.q: A government wants to sequester carbon on degraded land. Option A is a plantation of a fast-growing non-native conifer, harvested every 40 years. Option B is to allow native woodland to regenerate naturally. Scientists disagree about which is better. Which statement about this debate is justified?
items.correct: The plantation sequesters carbon faster at first, but native woodland may store more in the long term, so the evidence does not settle the question.
items.misconception: The plantation is certainly better, because the fastest rate of tree growth gives the greatest amount of carbon sequestered.
items.why: Rate of growth is easy to measure and to reason from, and students assume that a scientific question of this kind has a single settled answer. Plantations sequester carbon rapidly at first, but native woodland may store more carbon in the long term, including in soil, is less likely to be harvested and supports greater biodiversity. Which approach is best is a matter of active scientific debate.
items.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
items.random_wrong: Both options lock the carbon away permanently once the trees grow, so the only real difference between them is the cost.

items.q: Which statement about phenology is correct?
items.correct: It investigates the timing of biological events such as budburst, flowering and migration.
items.misconception: It investigates how the environment alters the phenotype of an organism during its lifetime.
items.why: The word resembles 'phenotype', and both are met in biology courses with little else to distinguish them. Phenology is research into the timing of biological events and the variables, such as photoperiod and temperature, that influence that timing.
items.specStatementText: Phenology: what sets the timing of the seasons' events
items.random_wrong: It shows that temperature is the cue for every seasonal event in every species.

items.q: A migratory bird species arrives at its northern breeding grounds on almost the same date every year, whether the spring is warm or cold. In the same region, the date of budburst in birch trees varies by up to three weeks between years. What can be concluded about the cues?
items.correct: Migration is cued mainly by photoperiod, whereas budburst is cued mainly by temperature
items.misconception: Both are cued by temperature, but the birds respond to it much less strongly than the trees
items.why: Warm weather is what students notice about spring, and the plants and animals that respond to a warm spell are the ones they see. Photoperiod and temperature patterns are examples of variables that influence the timing of biological events. Bud set in deciduous trees and the migration of many birds are cued mainly by photoperiod; budburst and flowering in many plants are cued mainly by temperature.
items.specStatementText: Phenology: what sets the timing of the seasons' events
items.random_wrong: Both are cued by photoperiod, which varies between years according to the spring weather

items.q: In the Arctic, spring growth of the mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium arcticum) is triggered by rising temperature, whereas the migration of reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) to their calving grounds is triggered by increasing day length. Springs are now warmer and earlier. What is the expected effect?
items.correct: Peak plant growth occurs before the calves are born, so they have less food
items.misconception: Both events advance by the same number of days, so synchrony between them is maintained
items.why: Students think of a season as a single event that arrives earlier for everything in the ecosystem at once. Spring growth of Arctic mouse-ear chickweed is cued by temperature and now occurs earlier, whereas reindeer migration is cued by photoperiod and has not advanced, so calves are born after the peak of plant growth. Different cues mean different responses.
items.specStatementText: When the cues disagree, synchrony breaks
items.random_wrong: The reindeer switch to using temperature as their cue and arrive earlier to match the plants

items.q: The spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus) completes one generation per year in cool summers but two or three in warm summers. In a region where mean summer temperature has risen by 2 °C, the area of spruce forest killed by the beetle has increased greatly. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Faster development at higher temperatures allows more generations per year, so beetle numbers build up more rapidly.
items.misconception: The number of generations per year is fixed genetically, so the extra damage must be due to beetles moving in from elsewhere.
items.why: Life cycles are taught as fixed sequences of stages with set durations, and the number of generations is stated as a species characteristic. Insects are ectotherms whose development from egg to adult speeds up as temperature rises. The spruce bark beetle completes one generation per year in cool conditions but two or three in warm ones, so warming increases the number of life cycles within a year.
items.specStatementText: More insect generations per year
items.random_wrong: Adult beetles live longer in the warmth, so each one attacks more trees over the course of its lifetime.

items.q: In Finland, tawny owls (Strix aluco) occur as a grey morph and a brown morph, and the colour is inherited. Brown owls survived snowy winters less well than grey owls. Between 1981 and 2008 winters became milder with less snow, and the proportion of brown owls rose from about 30% to about 50%. What best explains the change?
items.correct: The fitness of the brown morph rose as snow cover fell, so brown alleles increased in frequency by natural selection.
items.misconception: Individual grey owls gradually became browner over the years, as their plumage no longer needed to match snow in winter.
items.why: Students know of animals that change colour seasonally, such as Arctic hares, and of Lamarck's idea that individuals adapt and pass on the change. Tawny owl colour morph is genetically determined and does not change during an individual's life. Evolution is a change in the population: as snow cover decreased, the fitness of the brown morph rose and the brown allele became more common through natural selection.
items.specStatementText: Tawny owls: evolution within decades
items.random_wrong: Mutations producing brown plumage occurred more often once the winter snow cover had gone from the region.

items.q: The proportion of brown tawny owls (Strix aluco) in a population has risen over three decades as winter snow cover has decreased. Which statement about this change is correct?
items.correct: It is evolution, because the frequency of the brown allele in the population has changed.
items.misconception: It is not evolution, because evolution takes many thousands of years to produce any change.
items.why: Evolution is taught through the fossil record and the geological timescale, so students associate it only with very long periods. Evolution is a change in the heritable characteristics of a population. The rise in the brown morph of the tawny owl from about 30% to about 50% over three decades is evolution driven by changing snow cover, observed within a human lifetime.
items.specStatementText: Tawny owls: evolution within decades
items.random_wrong: It is not evolution, because the individual owls changed their colour to suit the milder conditions.

items.q: Is the hole in the ozone layer a cause of global warming?
items.correct: No. Anthropogenic climate change is caused by increased atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases, principally carbon dioxide and methane, which absorb long-wave radiation emitted by the Earth's surface.
items.misconception: Global warming is caused mainly by the hole in the ozone layer letting more of the Sun's heat reach the Earth.
items.why: Ozone depletion and climate change were both prominent environmental problems in the same lessons and news reports, both involve the atmosphere and gases released by humans, so students merge them into a single story. Ozone depletion and the enhanced greenhouse effect are different problems with different causes. Warming is caused by carbon dioxide and methane absorbing long-wave radiation re-emitted by the Earth, not by extra sunlight passing through a thinner ozone layer.
items.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is methane released by burning fossil fuels in the same way as carbon dioxide?
items.correct: No. Complete combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide; anthropogenic methane comes from enteric fermentation in livestock, rice paddies, landfill and leakage during the extraction and transport of fossil fuels.
items.misconception: All greenhouse gases are products of combustion, so methane, like carbon dioxide, is released mainly by burning fuels.
items.why: Combustion is the source of greenhouse gas that students meet first and most often, so they generalize it to every greenhouse gas. Methane is itself a fuel that is consumed by combustion. Its anthropogenic sources are biological (methanogenic archaea in the guts of ruminants, in rice paddies and in landfill) and leakage of natural gas, not the burning of fuels.
items.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a negative correlation a weak correlation?
items.correct: No. The sign of a correlation describes its direction, not its strength; a negative correlation can be as strong as a positive one.
items.misconception: A negative correlation is a weak or unreliable correlation, and a positive correlation is a strong one.
items.why: The everyday meanings of 'positive' (good, definite) and 'negative' (bad, doubtful) are carried over to the statistical terms. Positive and negative describe the direction of a correlation. Strength is a separate property: a perfect negative correlation is just as strong as a perfect positive one.
items.specStatementText: What humans have added to the atmosphere
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the methane and carbon dioxide released from thawing permafrost come from?
items.correct: From present-day decomposition by saprotrophs and methanogens of organic matter that stayed undecomposed while it was frozen.
items.misconception: The gases come from ancient pockets of gas trapped in the ice, which escape as it melts.
items.why: Ice cores are described as containing trapped bubbles of ancient air, and students transfer this image to permafrost. Permafrost contains huge amounts of undecomposed organic matter. When it thaws, decomposition that had been prevented by freezing begins: aerobic decomposition releases carbon dioxide and anaerobic decomposition by methanogens in waterlogged ground releases methane.
items.specStatementText: Feedbacks that make warming feed itself
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is a tipping point?
items.correct: A threshold beyond which an ecosystem shifts abruptly to a different state that may not be reversible.
items.misconception: A tipping point is just the point at which a gradual change begins, and the ecosystem will slowly return to normal once conditions improve.
items.why: The everyday phrase 'tipping point' is used loosely for any turning point, and students expect ecosystems to recover as they do in simple succession diagrams. Beyond a tipping point a small additional change causes a large, abrupt shift to a new state, such as a boreal forest becoming a net carbon source, and positive feedback can prevent a return to the original state even if the driver is reduced.
items.specStatementText: Boreal forest: from carbon sink to carbon source
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does melting sea ice raise sea level?
items.correct: No, or only negligibly: sea ice is already floating and displaces its own mass of water, so its melting does not raise sea level. Sea-level rise comes from thermal expansion and melting of land ice.
items.misconception: Melting sea ice raises sea level, so the threat to polar animals is the flooding of their breeding grounds.
items.why: Sea-level rise is the best-known consequence of melting ice in the news, and students do not distinguish floating sea ice from land-based glaciers and ice sheets. Floating ice displaces a volume of water equal to its own mass, so its melting leaves sea level essentially unchanged. The threat from melting sea ice and landfast ice is the loss of a platform for breeding and resting, not flooding.
items.specStatementText: Polar ice as habitat: emperor penguins and walruses
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do phytoplankton get the nutrients they need?
items.correct: From dissolved mineral ions such as nitrate and phosphate, which are brought to the surface from deep water by upwelling; light supplies energy, not nutrients.
items.misconception: Plants and phytoplankton get their nutrients from sunlight, so production is limited by light rather than by nutrients brought up from the deep ocean.
items.why: Sunlight is described as what plants 'need to grow', and 'nutrient' and 'energy' are merged into the idea of food, so the mineral ions needed for growth are overlooked. Light provides the energy for photosynthesis, but phytoplankton also need mineral nutrients. In the sunlit surface layer these are quickly used up and are replenished mainly by upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water, which is why changes in upwelling control ocean primary production.
items.specStatementText: Warm surface water blocks nutrient upwelling
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a species simply move with the climate and be unaffected?
items.correct: Not necessarily: mountain-top species run out of higher ground, land area decreases with altitude, and slow-dispersing species may not keep pace, so range shifts often involve range contraction.
items.misconception: As long as a species can shift its range, it is unaffected by warming because it keeps the same size of range.
items.why: Diagrams of range shift show a band of the same width moving up a slope or across a map, hiding the loss of area at the top of a mountain or the slow pace at which trees disperse. The area of a mountain decreases towards the summit, so a species shifting upslope occupies less area and species already at the top have nowhere to go. Trees spread only as fast as their seeds disperse, so the southern edge may retreat faster than the northern edge advances.
items.specStatementText: Species move poleward and upslope
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does ocean acidification make seawater acidic?
items.correct: No. Surface seawater pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 and remains alkaline; 'acidification' means a decrease in pH, not a pH below 7.
items.misconception: Ocean acidification means the sea has become acidic, with a pH below 7, and this acid dissolves the corals.
items.why: The word 'acidification' is read as 'becoming an acid', and students know that acids react with calcium carbonate. The oceans have become less alkaline, not acidic. The harm to corals comes from the reduced concentration of carbonate ions, which suppresses calcification, so corals build their calcium carbonate skeletons more slowly.
items.specStatementText: Coral reefs: acidification and bleaching
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are afforestation and forest regeneration the same thing?
items.correct: No. Afforestation is planting trees on land not recently forested; forest regeneration is the regrowth of forest on land that was previously forested.
items.misconception: Afforestation, reforestation and forest regeneration all mean planting trees, so they are the same approach.
items.why: The three terms are used interchangeably in everyday reports about tree planting. Afforestation creates forest on land that did not recently have it; forest regeneration is the natural or assisted regrowth of forest where it was cleared. Both sequester carbon in biomass and soil, but they are different approaches.
items.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is peat formed by compression of plant remains?
items.correct: No. Peat is partially decomposed plant material that accumulates because anaerobic waterlogged conditions inhibit decomposition; compression is not required.
items.misconception: Peat forms when layers of dead plants are compressed under water and sediment, in the same way as coal forms.
items.why: Coal formation is taught as compression of plant remains over millions of years, and peat is described as the first stage of that sequence. Peat accumulates at the surface of waterlogged soils within decades to centuries because decomposers cannot break the plant material down without oxygen. Compression and heat only come into play much later in coal formation.
items.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is carbon sequestered by trees locked away permanently?
items.correct: No. It is returned to the atmosphere if the trees are harvested and the wood decomposes or is burnt, or if the forest burns.
items.misconception: Once a tree has taken up carbon, that carbon is stored for ever.
items.why: Trees are presented as carbon sinks, and students do not follow the carbon after the tree dies or is cut down. Sequestration lasts only as long as the carbon stays in biomass, soil or peat. Harvesting, decomposition and fire return the carbon to the atmosphere, which is one reason long-lived native forest and re-wetted peatland are argued to be better long-term stores than harvested plantations.
items.specStatementText: Sequestering carbon in forests and peat

items.q: Does photoperiod change as the climate warms?
items.correct: No. Day length at a given latitude and date is fixed by the Earth's orbit and tilt, so it is unaffected by climate change.
items.misconception: As the climate warms, the days get longer earlier in the year, so photoperiod cues shift along with temperature cues.
items.why: Longer days and warmer weather arrive together each spring, so students treat them as a single 'season' signal that warming brings forward. Photoperiod follows an unchanging annual pattern. Events cued by photoperiod therefore keep to the same dates while events cued by temperature shift earlier, which is why climate change disrupts synchrony between them.
items.specStatementText: Phenology: what sets the timing of the seasons' events

items.q: Will a population immediately correct a phenological mismatch by changing its cue?
items.correct: No. The cue a population responds to is largely heritable; changing it requires natural selection over generations, and meanwhile the mismatch reduces breeding success.
items.misconception: Organisms will simply adjust: if the reindeer arrive too late, they will start using temperature as their cue and arrive earlier next year.
items.why: Students attribute conscious or deliberate adjustment to organisms, and expect a mismatch to be self-correcting because it is obviously disadvantageous. A population responds to the cue its genes have been selected to use. Individuals cannot switch cue at will, so mismatch persists and reduces fitness until, over generations, selection changes the response.
items.specStatementText: When the cues disagree, synchrony breaks

items.q: Why does warming allow the spruce bark beetle to complete more life cycles in a year?
items.correct: Because development from egg to adult is faster at higher temperatures, so each generation takes less time and more fit into the season.
items.misconception: Insects live longer in warm weather, so each beetle has time to reproduce more times in a year.
items.why: Students confuse the length of an individual's life with the time taken to complete a generation, and assume warmth extends life. Warmth shortens the time from egg to reproductive adult rather than lengthening life. The season is the same length, so shorter generation times mean more generations, larger populations and more damage to spruce forests.
items.specStatementText: More insect generations per year

items.q: Did the decrease in snow cover cause new mutations for brown plumage in tawny owls?
items.correct: No. Both colour morphs already existed; the environmental change altered their relative fitness, and selection changed the frequency of existing alleles.
items.misconception: Environmental change causes the mutations that organisms need, so less snow produced the brown allele.
items.why: Students see mutation as a response to need, because in the story of adaptation the useful variant appears just when it is required. Mutation is random with respect to need. The brown and grey alleles were both present before winters changed; what changed was which morph survived better, so natural selection increased the frequency of the brown allele.
items.specStatementText: Tawny owls: evolution within decades
